extracted.intended_audience: mathematics instructors and graduate TAs who design assessments and grade student work
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for assessing and providing feedback on undergraduate mathematics student work (homework, reports, team projects, and writing assignments), including rubric design, feedback tone, and issues specific to mathematical writing and group work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear and precise communication of mathematical ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: A common element of these assessment practices is the clear and precise communication of mathematical ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage students to exhibit understanding in multiple ways (such as graphs, written accounts of their assumptions and reasoning processes) instead of simply recording algebraic steps and boxed answers. Assess the clarity and precision of exposition as part of the grade.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design of cooperative/group assignments
rubrics_metrics.description: Problems assigned to groups should be more complicated and sometimes more 'open-ended' than traditional exercises to provide sufficient challenge and incentive for cooperative work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such problems should require students to make appropriate assumptions, try alternative avenues of inquiry, and recognize applications to unfamiliar situations so groups cannot trivially divide and compile individual parts. When grading, consider how to reward genuine collaboration and how to handle uneven contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attach numeric grade to a meaningful unit (not nit-picking individual errors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Correct all errors, no matter how small, but the smallest unit to which a number should be attached is an exercise or a part of an exercise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid littering problems with -1/2 or -1 marks for each tiny error; instead correct as you go and then assign one number for the whole exercise or part. This reduces student complaints about 'nit-picking' and produces fairer scores.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frame scoring as giving points rather than deducting them
rubrics_metrics.description: Students often react better when you give them points rather than take them away.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For example, if an exercise is worth 8 points and the student misses two of those points, write 6 beside the exercise rather than writing -2. Using a 'give' system encourages instructors to think of overall worth rather than enumerating deductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone of written comments: avoid emphatic 'shouting' devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use emphatic devices such as underlining, capitalizing, and exclamation marks when making negative comments; these are written forms of shouting that can hurt students’ feelings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer neutral factual statements (e.g., 'This problem cannot be done this way since the function is not linear.') over emphatic versions ('This problem CANNOT be done this way since the function is NOT LINEAR!!!'). Positive comments may use emphasis, but avoid emphatic adjectives like 'obviously' when criticizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handle nonsense/bluffing neutrally
rubrics_metrics.description: When a student's write-up is nonsense or they are bluffing, convey the point neutrally rather than retaliating in tone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A neutral comment such as 'This is incorrect—see the examples given in class.' combined with the appropriate grade (possibly zero) is more effective than sarcastic or punitive remarks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use double-submission (draft & revision) to encourage processing feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Make some assignments 'double submission' where the first draft is commented on and the second draft is graded, with students required to submit a description of how they addressed each instructor comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This mirrors journal revision processes and helps students process comments individually. If full double submission is too burdensome, require it for the first one or two assignments as a compromise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write suggestions as questions and in complete sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggestions and comments are often more effective when framed as questions and written as complete sentences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Single-word comments are often misunderstood or not taken seriously. Asking guided questions can prompt student reflection and revision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a limited set of category labels rather than every numeric value
rubrics_metrics.description: Although you may grade on a numerical scale, you don't have to use every number; group papers into categories with representative scores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example mapping: Excellent paper — 20/20; 'Good' paper — 17/20; 'Needs Improvement' — 14/20; 'Poor' — ≤12/20. This can simplify grading and make distinctions clearer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess separate goals separately (presentation vs content)
rubrics_metrics.description: To the extent possible, evaluate students' success at separate goals separately (for example, 'writing' aspects and 'content' aspects).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presentation/communication/language aspects to assess include: relevant issues addressed directly, central ideas communicated effectively, logical order of arguments and discussion, acceptable style and grammar. Evidence of conceptual understanding to assess includes: clear understanding of important issues, awareness of implications of data, support of conclusions with references, connections among data/references, and conclusions that follow from information and arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide summary of good points and points for improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: A summary of good points and points of improvement at the end of the paper can be very helpful for students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such summaries are especially useful when systemic problems or student style issues exist; they can be time-consuming to write but are high-value feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance positive feedback with constructive criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Students need both positive feedback and constructive criticism: they need to know what they did right as well as where they can improve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure comments include both affirmation of strengths and concrete guidance for improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic rubrics (broad, intuition-based grading scheme)
rubrics_metrics.description: Generic rubrics are very generic grading schemes that apply to grading almost any piece of student work; their consistent and fair use depends heavily on the instructor's ability to gain a general sense of 'quality'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generic rubrics allow fast grading if the instructor focuses on overall sense of quality rather than every detail. Example 5-point scale: 5 — intelligent, thoughtful work (not necessarily perfect); 3 — serious write-up problems but good mathematics or a seriously flawed approach written up well; 1 — minimal effort or no concept; 0 — no work submitted. Scores 4 and 2 are used when between categories. Advantages: quick to create and apply, fast scoring; Disadvantages: provides little specific feedback unless comments are added, relies on instructor intuition, susceptible to fatigue changes and superficial grading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific rubrics (assignment- or problem-specific)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific rubrics apply to a particular style of assignment, a particular assignment, or even a single problem; they are concrete and explicit about points awarded or deducted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good for new instructors because they are concrete. Process for creating a specific rubric (illustrated in Figure 1): decide total points, work the problem as expected students would, examine your solution to find critical assumptions/steps/results, divide up the available points among those elements, look back at the rubric to ensure it rewards what is important and is 'just,' and try to anticipate alternative student approaches and how you'll handle them. Specific rubrics help consistency and speed but can be unjust if applied too rigidly and require effort to create and to handle unusual answers or different valid interpretations.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Look back' and fairness check when designing rubrics
rubrics_metrics.description: After creating a rubric, review it to ensure your sense of what is important hasn't been 'lost in the details' and that the rubric is 'just' (e.g., prevents one small error from lowering an otherwise excellent score disproportionately).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the 'looking back' step to revise point allocations and consider fairness across common student mistakes and alternative valid approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate and handle alternative valid student approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: When designing rubrics, try to anticipate some alternative methods students might use and think about how you will handle these situations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review samples of student work (if available) before finalizing the rubric; you may need more than one rubric if students interpret the problem in very different but valid ways.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment issues specific to student mathematical writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Reading, commenting, and evaluating mathematical writing can be time-consuming; instructors must decide how much to 'read students' minds' (infer unstated assumptions) and whether poor exposition reflects lack of understanding or unfamiliarity with writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious about attributing omissions to misunderstanding vs. stylistic/expressive limits. Consider whether to score spelling/grammar/paragraphing/style and how these interact with mathematical understanding. Use double submission or guided revision when appropriate to help distinguish content problems from writing skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plagiarism and collaboration considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Be alert to plagiarism in several ways: failure to properly reference quoted material, extent of collaboration on team homework and projects, and file-sharing via word processors that makes authorship unclear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be clear to students ahead of time about acceptable collaboration and referencing. Note that blatant large-scale plagiarism is rare, but instructors should set explicit policies and consider process-based safeguards (e.g., drafts, reflections) to verify authorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency in grading (across students and assignments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain consistency both between students on a given assignment and across different assignments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using rubrics (generic or specific), keeping exemplar 'excellent/fair/poor' papers as references, and grading in batches while fresh can improve reliability. Beware of fatigue-related drift in judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use exemplar papers and memory aids to improve grading reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose examples of 'excellent,' 'fair,' and 'poor' papers and keep these aside as an aide to memory when grading essay questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This technique (recommended by McKeachie) can help maintain consistency and serve as a quick reference for borderline cases, though it adds upfront work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checklist approach for grading mathematical essays (time-efficient explicit checklist)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some systems grade writing assignments according to an explicit checklist (e.g., an eleven-point checklist) which can be time-efficient and concrete for inexperienced graders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Checklists provide concrete criteria and can speed grading, but instructors should ensure they address both content and exposition. Meier & Rishel suggest items to check such as clear introduction/conclusion, organization, clarity of arguments, indication of why calculations are performed, and clear mathematical arguments.
